items.label: Human
items.text: At first, it’s deliberate, even awkward.

paragraphs.before: Reparenting means consciously evolving and molding an Inner Adult inside you, comprising a loving Nurturer, a safe Adult Protector (hereafter just the Protector) and a wise Guide. This chosen Inner Adult super hero gets into a real, loving relationship with the little one you still carry. That grown-up notices the old patterns and practices better ways of responding.
paragraphs.window: At first, it’s deliberate, even awkward.
paragraphs.after: With time, the roles become second nature, so you spend less of your life managing yourself and more of it living with purpose, loving, relaxing, and playing.

items.label: Human
section: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
Five Stages of Reparenting

paragraphs.before: 1. You’re still stuck identifying as the lost inner child, forced frequently into handling situations that require more maturity, even if it looks like you’ve got it all together. At this stage, use your childlike superpowers to come into the “Wow of Now” (have you seen the movie Waking Life?), and make sure there’s enough safety around you to continue with reparenting:2. Begin to borrow adulthood — remember watching Mr. Rogers or Sesame Street? Those adult role models are what we’re looking for at this stage. This can almost feel like playing house as a kid where you imagined how you’d take care of a baby doll etc.
paragraphs.after: Practice adulting — do at least one part of caring for yourself while support is still there from the previous step.4. Adult mode itself — after sufficient practice with reparenting, you become a natural at sending love to little you, protecting them, and directing them. 5. Adult and child in relationship — the adult leads. The child isn’t pushed away, but doesn’t have to run the whole life alone. This can actually feel really weird if you’ve been stuck in forced adulthood for a while. Our goal is to go from weird to silly and playful. Lose self-consciousness while gaining self-awareness, if that makes sense!

Signs of Manipulation

paragraphs.before: Some manipulative people are too smart to act perfect. They lead with their wounds, or with how brutally honest they are about their flaws (very disarming, which is sort of the point), and every warning you hear about them just becomes more proof of how deep they are.

Whoever’s noticing isn’t all the way inside the scared one.
It can help to use your own name.
section: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Noticing Counts

paragraphs.before: “Huh, somebody in here is really scared.” That might be the most adult thing you’ve got right now, and it’s plenty to start with.
paragraphs.window: Whoever’s noticing isn’t all the way inside the scared one.
It can help to use your own name.
paragraphs.after: For me, instead of “I’m terrified,” that’d be “Little Joel is terrified. What does Little Joel need right now?” You’ll sound a bit like Elmo :) In lab studies, though, people who talked to themselves this way reacted less to upsetting pictures and memories, and their brains didn’t seem to be working any harder to do it.

items.text: For protecting, ask what a minimally competent adult would do here.
section: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult

paragraphs.window: For protecting, ask what a minimally competent adult would do here.
paragraphs.after: Maybe something simple, like actually smelling that old food you’re about to eat and then trashing it if it smells a little weird. If you’re about to send an angry text, hit pause. If the room itself triggers your spidey sense, leave, or lock the door and get help. Even if this still feels like the child acting like the adult, for now, that’s ok. “Fake it til you make it” isn’t exactly it, but yeah. Afterward, you can tell your little one, “I did that for us. That was the Protector.” If it sounds funny, laugh!

section: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Remember When You Already Did It

paragraphs.before: My father often suggested folks remember a similar-level (or even harder) challenge that they were able to handle. Maybe you survived a car crash and surgery a few years ago, but now you’re having trouble with emotional eating. You can draw strength from the past. As my sister, a historian, likes to say, “The past didn’t go anywhere.” Your own challenge doesn’t need to be as dramatic as a car crash, as long as it really happened. So who or what helped you get through it? Is one piece of that still within reach? If you catch yourself thinking “I survived a car crash, so why can’t I stop eating when I’m upset?”, that’s the past turned into a stick to hit yourself with. Maybe you’re more worn out now, or missing whatever helped back then.

items.text: Set one boundary.
section: Building Trust With Your Little One
Not Every Hero Wears A Cape

paragraphs.window: Set one boundary.
paragraphs.after: “What’s a ‘boundary’?”, I might be asking. That looks like saying no to something that’s costing you too much (money, time, whatever it is). Handle that task you’ve been putting off, or the tax man, or your DUIs in Maryland, even if all you do today is open the envelope. Keep one small promise to your little one. Clean your room! Maybe your little one had grown-ups who said sweet things and then did nothing, and maybe you’ve done it too, so this is how they start to believe you.

items.text: So the anger seemed stupid.
section: Building Trust With Your Little One
Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust ❤️

paragraphs.before: That completely threw me. Fights don’t usually go like that. Anger is a way to get more power when you feel a lack of justice or agency. You puff yourself up so you seem frightening or dangerous, or you demand to be heard. My anger was there to get me heard, and her answer showed me I didn’t need it for that. Whatever injustice I thought there was wasn’t coming from a lack of love, either.
paragraphs.window: So the anger seemed stupid.
paragraphs.after: I saw for myself that it was only hurting me, without helping me see clearly or get what I wanted. Still, what I screamed was true right then, and what she said back was true too, so I could hate somebody who loved me and she’d still be my mom the whole time.

items.text:
Pick a memory you can handle for the first few tries.
Does saying it make the memory fiction?
section: Simple Practices
“And So That’s the Way It Happened!”

paragraphs.before: My ex, Xandria, taught me to append “And so that’s the way it happened!” to a difficult memory. Say it the way a grandpa would finish a story on the porch. (”Once upon a time…” helps if the start is where you get stuck.) Somehow it moves the whole thing out of the courtroom, where the case was still being argued, and into your life story.
paragraphs.window: Pick a memory you can handle for the first few tries.
Does saying it make the memory fiction?
paragraphs.after: Well, no, it’s still what happened, as far as you remember it, even if some details turn out fuzzy. If the phrase does the trick, leave it at that, no need to narrate the whole thing.

paragraphs.window: Do keep an ear on who’s narrating, though.
paragraphs.after: If the voice starts sneering, like it’s making fun of the younger you, stop right there (that’s the courtroom creeping back in). Same if you feel more ashamed, or kind of floaty and unreal, since more distance won’t help with that. And when it goes well, it’s a good time to check in with the younger you in that story. What do they need from you now?

paragraphs.before: A new roommate doesn’t win you over with a speech on move-in day (hopefully, right?). The rent just has to keep showing up. Your Protector earns that guard’s trust about the same way, mostly out in ordinary life.
paragraphs.window: The things you do can be small, like keeping a promise to yourself nobody else knew about. Or saying no to someone, and not texting an hour later to take it back. That second one can be really hard.
That part doesn’t have to move out. It’s been living there way longer than the grown-up you.
paragraphs.after: It can keep watch while you take one small step toward your little one, and I think watching is what it wants anyway, to find out if there’s a grown-up here now who could call it off if things got to be too much. It doesn’t have to be all or nothing, either. Maybe it would settle for a lighter cover for now, like blinds tilted open a crack, and let you peek out for a minute (ST-CA, section 9.3.4). If it says no, I’d listen. When it lets you, keep an eye on that part too, for any change at all. If it’s been calling all this stupid, it might turn out to be scared of getting its hopes up. I wouldn’t want to get mine up either. I’d tell it something like, “You don’t have to hope yet, I’ll keep coming back even when I mess up.” Sometimes it doesn’t say anything back for a while.

paragraphs.after: Well, not the mainstream kind, but yes, for sure. Professional therapy’s still useful for what it does, and peers and community do something else, so a serious healing path can include both.

items.label: Human
items.text: They still have to answer for what they did, and it still hurt.
section: How to Forgive Without Forgetting

paragraphs.window: They still have to answer for what they did, and it still hurt.
paragraphs.after: Seeing how they got there doesn’t make it okay. It’s just that punishing them now can’t reach back and give them what they were missing then, the sense to see it or the help. Or the skills. What’s left is fixing what can be fixed, and making it easier for something different to happen now. So a boundary can still be right. So can the law, if it comes to that, or telling them plainly it was wrong (or telling yourself, if they’d never hear it). Keeping away from them for good can be right too, and you can still forgive them from over there. Understanding somebody’s limitations should make my expectations more realistic, not make those limitations less consequential. “I understand how you became this way” can sit right next to “I now understand why I shouldn’t rely on you for this.”

items.label: Human
items.text: Changing the behavior counts too.
section: How to Forgive Without Forgetting
Forgiving Yourself

paragraphs.before: Forgiving yourself works the same way. Own what you did (only what was yours), and let yourself feel the remorse. Repair what you can, by apologizing or making amends.
paragraphs.window: Changing the behavior counts too.
paragraphs.after: Then you’re allowed to stop holding yourself hostage, and the responsibility stays. If you’re thinking “not me, not after what I did,” forgiving other people tends to be harder too. Every so often, come back to how whoever did it got to be someone who could do that, until you understand it well enough that it changes how you feel.

items.label: Human
items.text: Is it?
section: When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun

paragraphs.before: Your little one might be sure everything’s over.
paragraphs.window: Is it?
paragraphs.after: Usually one real thing ended, and there’s other stuff you’re still trying to keep going, maybe on autopilot. Some of it just isn’t known yet, and unknown isn’t the same as gone. Ask your little one what they’re scared will happen in the meantime (worst-case scenarios are kind of their specialty).

items.text: Love from a person is more conditional than that.
section: You Are Worthy of Love. Always.

paragraphs.before: It’s the same love as back in Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED!, the Divine Love that can start as a little spark of … something when you give thanks. That kind, whether you’d say it comes from God or the universe itself or whatever, was there before you could earn anything.
paragraphs.window: Love from a person is more conditional than that.
paragraphs.after: Somebody’s love running out on you still says nothing about what you’re worth.

items.label: Human
items.text: It sets limits, too.
section: Appendix
How This Relates to Schema Therapy

paragraphs.before: Of the clinical approaches I know, schema therapy is the closest to this guide. Its therapists do what they call limited reparenting: within professional limits, they give you some of what a good parent would, with warmth and firmness and some playfulness too. Over time you take that in, and it becomes your own “Healthy Adult,” who looks after your “Vulnerable Child” and stands up to the punishing parent in your head.
paragraphs.window: It sets limits, too.
paragraphs.after: And it gets on with adult life, like work and the things you’ve committed to. Sound familiar? That’s a Nurturer, a Protector and a Guide by other names, and since the therapist’s version becomes yours bit by bit, it’s borrowed adulthood too.

items.label: Human
items.text: Where it really differs is spirituality.
section: Appendix
How This Relates to Schema Therapy

paragraphs.window: Where it really differs is spirituality.
paragraphs.after: Schema therapy doesn’t build it in, though the preface to its main textbook calls blending it with meditation or religious practice an important development. That’s not so surprising, since it grew out of cognitive therapy. Some people do blend them, though. Tara Bennett-Goleman’s book Emotional Alchemy, for one, fits a Buddhist loving-kindness wish to each schema. Her book barely mentions gratitude, and for me that’s the door to the bigger love back in Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED! IFS goes overboard the other way, in my opinion (more on that in the next section).

items.text: It can’t act like some transcendent authority that waves everything away.
section: Appendix
How This Relates to IFS

paragraphs.before: So inner child therapy draws on those higher vantage points more concretely. The inner Guide is the closest thing here to a Higher Self, and it has to work with the Nurturer and Protector and come after them.
paragraphs.window: It can’t act like some transcendent authority that waves everything away.
paragraphs.after: Most reparenting doesn’t do enough with the Guide, which is the opposite extreme from IFS, so I’m trying to bring together the best of both. IFS isn’t exactly one system, so I may be simplifying it here. It has its own branches and disputes, and that’s one more problem I’m trying to remedy by laying all this out systematically in this guide.
